To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have cloned a rat homologue of KCNQ2 channel, which shares 96% identity with human KCQ2. rKCNK2 is expressed in rat brain and is functional.
we have isolated a novel K(+) channel gene from rat brain and characterized the functional expression of the gene in a cell culture system.

we have cloned a novel K(+) channel gene, rKCN0, from a rat cDNA library using the RACE technique and that we have functionally expressed rKCN0 in an HEK-293 cell line by patch clamp recording and in Xenopous oocytes by two electrode voltage clamp recording.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular biology and physiology of the K(+) channels, which are involved in the control of neuronal excitability and are important targets for the treatment of epilepsy and pain.
the identification and molecular cloning of a novel voltage-gated potassium channel, rKcnq2, from rat brain.
the identification and characterization of a new K(+) channel subfamily.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
rKCNQ1 is a voltage-gated potassium channel, which is expressed in rat brain and is a member of the KCNQ family.
rKCNQ1, rKCNH2, rKCNJ2, rKCNN1, and rKCNN2 are all cloned and expressed in the laboratory of the author.
KCNQ2 channels play an important role in the regulation of excitability and that their dysfunction may contribute to the pathogenesis of epilepsy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have cloned a new voltage-gated K channel from rat brain, rKCN2, and have shown its functional expression.
we cloned the rKCNQ gene and found its expression in the brain and its function in a voltage-gated potassium channel.
we have cloned and functionally expressed the rKCNQ1 gene from a rat brain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we identified the first rodent member of the KCNQ subfamily of K(+) channels.
the cloned rKCNQ channel has a delayed rectifier type of current, which is consistent with the previous work done on the human KCNQ channels.
the rKCNQ channel is an important regulator of K+ channel currents and that it may serve as a potential target for therapeutic intervention in the treatment of epilepsy.
